Done. Both `analysis.py` and `result.json` are written.

## Answer to H2: No

Default `RandomForestClassifier()` does **not** beat default `LogisticRegression()` here — it is slightly worse.

| | Stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC |
|---|---|
| LogisticRegression() | **0.9053** |
| RandomForestClassifier() | 0.9016 |
| **Difference (RF − LR)** | **−0.0037** |

## Verification

All three checks agreed:
- **5×repeated 5-fold CV (25 paired folds):** mean diff −0.0035; RF won only **1 of 25** folds. Bootstrap 95% CI **[−0.0043, −0.0028]**, excluding zero.
- **Untouched 80/20 hold-out:** RF 0.9048 vs LR 0.9080 (−0.0032) — same sign and size, though its own row-bootstrap CI [−0.0073, +0.0008] straddles zero. A single 9,769-row test set can't resolve a 0.003 gap; the paired 25-fold comparison can.

## Two forks worth flagging

Neither model is really "better" — both sit at ~0.90 AUC, and the sign of a 0.004 gap depends on preprocessing choices that were mine to make:

1. **Scaling is the decisive one.** Left unscaled, default `LogisticRegression()` (lbfgs, `max_iter=100`) never converges and collapses to **0.668** AUC — which would flip the headline into a huge apparent RF win of +0.234. That number is an artifact of a truncated optimizer, not a model-class difference. A researcher who skipped scaling would confidently report the opposite conclusion.
2. **Encoding flips the sign, but not the substance.** Under ordinal instead of one-hot categoricals, RF rises to 0.9060 — a paired diff of **+0.0008**, CI [+0.0000, +0.0015]. Statistically distinguishable from zero, practically a dead heat.

So the sign of the RF−LogReg gap is *not* robust to encoding, and I've said so in `result.json` rather than reporting the one-hot number alone. Under no defensible preprocessing does RF show a meaningful advantage.

One process note: my first run backgrounded itself on the 600s cap (25 sequential RF fits at ~16s each); I parallelized the fold loop and re-ran it to completion in the foreground. I had also pre-written the summary strings assuming RF would win — those were wrong and are rewritten to match the actual numbers.

parsed_result.summary: No. With identical in-fold preprocessing (median/most-frequent imputation, standardized numerics, one-hot categoricals), default RandomForestClassifier() reaches a stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC of 0.9016 versus 0.9053 for default LogisticRegression() -- a difference of -0.0037, i.e. the forest is very slightly WORSE. The gap is tiny in absolute terms (both models sit at ~0.90 AUC) but consistent: logistic regression won 24 of 25 folds under repeated CV. The verdict is sensitive to encoding, though -- with ordinal instead of one-hot encoded categoricals the forest matches logistic regression (+0.0008), so the honest reading is that these two defaults are practically tied on this dataset, with no RF advantage.
parsed_result.direction: RF < LogReg (no RF advantage; difference ~-0.004 AUC, practically a tie)
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Estimators left at literal sklearn defaults as specified (RandomForestClassifier(): 100 trees, unlimited depth; LogisticRegression(): lbfgs, L2, C=1.0, max_iter=100); only random_state was set on RF for reproducibility. Both models were fed the IDENTICAL feature matrix so the comparison isolates model class: median imputation + StandardScaler on the 6 numeric columns, most-frequent imputation + one-hot (handle_unknown='ignore') on the 8 categoricals; all fit inside each training fold via a Pipeline to avoid leakage. Scaling is inert for a forest but is what lets default LogisticRegression converge within max_iter=100 -- another researcher who skipped scaling would compare against a non-converged LR. Missing values ('?' -> NaN in workclass/occupation/native-country) were imputed rather than dropped or coded as their own level. fnlwgt (the census sampling weight) was retained as a predictor. No de-duplication. Class imbalance (23.9% positive) left untouched -- ROC-AUC is threshold-free and class_weight/resampling would depart from 'defaults'. Metric: ROC-AUC on predict_proba, StratifiedKFold with shuffle=True, random_state=42. TWO FORKS MATERIALLY CHANGE THE ANSWER and another researcher could easily land elsewhere: (a) Scaling. If the numerics are left unscaled, default LogisticRegression() does not converge in max_iter=100 and collapses to 0.6677 AUC, which would flip the conclusion to a large apparent RF win of +0.2339. That number is an artifact of a non-converged optimizer, not a real model-class difference, which is why I scale. (b) Encoding. With ordinal instead of one-hot categoricals the forest improves to 0.9057 single-run / 0.9060 under repeated CV, a paired difference vs LR of +0.0008 (95% CI [+0.0000, +0.0015]) -- a statistical dead heat rather than an RF win. So the sign of the RF-LogReg gap is not robust to encoding, but under no defensible preprocessing does RF show a meaningful advantage.
parsed_result.verification_method: Three independent checks: (1) 5x repeated stratified 5-fold CV with fresh split seeds and a fresh RF seed per fold (25 paired folds); (2) a 10,000-draw percentile bootstrap 95% CI on the mean paired per-fold AUC difference; (3) refit on an 80/20 stratified hold-out split (random_state=2024) never used in the primary analysis, with a 2,000-draw paired-row bootstrap CI on the test-set AUC difference.
parsed_result.verification_result: The finding held up in direction and magnitude. Repeated CV: RF 0.9017 (sd 0.0036) vs LogReg 0.9053 (sd 0.0031), mean paired difference -0.0035; RF was ahead in only 1/25 folds, so LogReg won 24/25. Bootstrap 95% CI of the mean paired difference [-0.0043, -0.0028], excluding zero. Untouched 80/20 hold-out reproduced the same sign and size: RF 0.9048 vs LogReg 0.9080, difference -0.0032, though its paired-row bootstrap CI [-0.0073, +0.0008] does straddle zero -- a single 9,769-row test set cannot resolve a 0.003 AUC gap, whereas the 25-fold paired comparison can. Revised estimate: RF is worse by about 0.0035 AUC, range ~[-0.0043, -0.0028] under one-hot encoding; under ordinal encoding the gap shrinks to +0.0008 ([+0.0000, +0.0015]), i.e. a tie. In no variant did RF beat LogReg by a practically meaningful margin, so the answer to H2 as posed is No.
